Hello! We are Piyasa Team.

We aim to join this outstanding competition, gain experience, and grow together. Our goal is to develop a practical solution that helps our planet and builds a better future.

We specialize in agriculture and weather forecasting, using our knowledge and creativity to solve real-world challenges.

We hope this competition is memorable for all competitors and everyone who organizes and supports it.

Thank you for this opportunity!

Sincerely,
Piyasa Team We look ahead.
summary:
Earth.exe is an interactive web tool that makes climate change easier to understand. It combines two important features, a climate map and a crop finder. On the map, users can explore heat changes for any place in the world, compare past and future periods, and pick specific years and months and different situations. The crop finder lets users choose a veraity of plants and a locations, then it shows whether it can grow there and how that changes over time.
The project addresses the challenge by turning complex climate data into something anyone can explore. Instead of reading reports users can click a place and immediately see what its climate looks like.
This matters because climate change is already affecting agriculture and farming. Farmers and students need clear, local information to plan ahead. Earth.exe makes that information accessible and interactive.
details:
1. Summary (ready to paste into the form)

Earth.exe is a browser-based climate and crop-planning tool. People spin a 3D globe, choose a climate scenario (from “Best case” to “Worst case”) and a time window up to 2100, and see how temperature, rain, frost, sunshine and soil wetness may change anywhere on Earth. In the Crop Finder, a farmer picks one of 39 crops, taps a place on the map, and gets the best sowing months, the expected yield in tons per hectare, and how that yield shifts from 1970–2000 to 2081–2100, with or without watering. It runs from a single HTML file with no server, no account and no data downloads. The current prototype uses a transparent, simplified climate model rather than raw NASA or CMIP6 files, and it is designed so that real datasets can be plugged in.

2. The problem

  • Farming is planned around a climate that is already moving. Planting calendars come from the experience of past decades, while frost dates, heat and rainfall keep shifting.
  • Climate projections exist but are hard to use. The IPCC scenarios (SSPs from CMIP6) are published as technical grids and codes such as SSP2-4.5. A farmer, a teacher or a local official cannot open them to answer a practical question.
  • The real question is practical: “What should I plant, in which months, and what can I expect to harvest in ten, thirty or seventy years?”
  • Earth.exe turns scenario science into that answer, in plain language, on any phone or laptop. It supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger) and Goal 13 (Climate Action).

3. What Earth.exe does

3.1 First run

  • A retro loading window (“Loading climate.dat…”, “Warming up the oceans…”, “Planting virtual crops…”, “Polishing pixels…”) fills a progress bar over three seconds.
  • The landing page shows the title, the tagline, a blinking PRESS START button and the label “Educational model · not real measured data”. A second screen offers two paths: Climate Map and Crop Finder.
  • Both pages have deep links (#climate and #crops), so a teacher can share a link that opens straight on the Crop Finder.

3.2 Climate Map

Time controls

  • Past or future? Past (1970–2000) plus four scenarios named in plain words: Best case (SSP1-2.6), Middle road (SSP2-4.5), High emissions (SSP3-7.0) and Worst case (SSP5-8.5).
  • Which years? 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080 or 2081–2100.
  • Which month? Annual, or any single month. “Play the year” animates through the months, one every 0.7 seconds.
  • Show change vs. the past switches to a difference map, so users see how much a place changes instead of absolute values.

Map controls

  • 3D globe or flat (Mercator) map, land-only view, a layer opacity slider, grid lines whose spacing adapts to zoom (30°, 10°, 5°, 1°) and a °C/°F switch.
  • Drag to rotate; wheel, pinch or double-click to zoom from 1× to 120×; zoom buttons, reset, fullscreen, a scale bar, and a live readout of coordinates and value under the cursor. Place labels appear when zoomed in.
  • Search by place name or by typing “lat, lon”: 41 named places (10 quick-pick chips plus 31 more) with an animated fly-to.
  • “World at a glance” cards show the area-weighted global mean and the maximum and minimum with their coordinates.

Place inspector (click anywhere)

  • A plain sentence: “Here it is about X °C on average, with Y mm of rain a year. In 2041–2060 it could be Z °C warmer and drier.”
  • Charts: monthly temperature for all five scenarios; monthly precipitation, past versus the selected scenario; and a weather-details chart with a table of the 11 derived layers (past → scenario, with the change).
  • Show data for this place prints a CSV (12 months of temperature and precipitation for every scenario, plus the 11 derived layers for the selected scenario) with a Copy button, for classrooms and further analysis.

3.3 Crop Finder

  • A search box and five category chips (Cereals, Vegetables, Legumes, Oil & Industrial, Fruits & Roots) over 39 crops shown as emoji tiles.
  • Picking a crop turns the map into a suitability map (red → yellow → green, 0–100 %). Tapping a land point gives that place’s result. The default location is the Zonguldak area, and ocean points return a friendly message.
  • Result card: a verdict badge (Excellent / Good / Possible / Poor here), the best sowing months, the expected yield in t/ha and as a percentage of the crop’s potential, a 12-month strip colored by sowing quality, local rain versus the crop’s water need with plain advice, five bars for 1970–2000 and the four future periods, and a trend sentence such as “Gets better by 2100” or “Becomes possible by 2100”.
  • A Rain only / With watering toggle. Scenario and years come from the same menu as the climate map, so a farmer can compare futures.
  • Every result reminds the user to ask a local farmer or agriculture office before planting.

3.4 Design

  • Plain language first. “Past or future?”, “Which years?” and “Show change vs. the past”, with scenario codes kept secondary.
  • A friendly retro-desktop look. Window title bars (earth.exe, crop_finder.exe), a taskbar with a Start button and clock, pixel-art sprites drawn from text grids as crisp SVG, and the Press Start 2P and VT323 fonts give a technical subject a memorable personality.
  • Responsive and accessible. The layout adapts from phones to wide screens (slide-in menu drawer, pinch zoom, safe-area insets). Animations stop for users who prefer reduced motion, icon buttons and the landing illustration carry aria labels, and Enter and Esc work as shortcuts.

3.5 Easter egg

Switching between the Climate and Crops tabs five times in a row unlocks an 8-bit theme (a Game Boy-style green palette with scanlines) and a mini-game, catch.exe: catch water drops, dodge smog, three lives, with speed rising as the score grows. Closing it plays a typewriter credit line, “TED Zonguldak Koleji sevgilerini sunar…”.

4. How the Crop Finder works

4.1 Crop database

4.2 Algorithm

For a chosen place, scenario and period, the model builds 12 monthly temperatures and rainfall values, then tests each of the 12 possible sowing months:

  1. Sowing gate. The sowing month’s mean temperature must be at least the minimum sowing temperature and no higher than the upper optimum plus 1 °C.
  2. Season walk. For each month of the growing season, if the mean temperature is below the killing temperature the yield is zero. Otherwise the month gets a temperature factor from the trapezoid, and its rain is added to the season total.
  3. Temperature score = the average temperature factor over the season.
  4. Water factor. Rain only: min(1, (season rain ÷ water requirement)^0.7). With watering: a fixed 0.97.
  5. Yield index = temperature score × water factor (0 to 1).
  6. Expected yield = yield index × the crop’s maximum yield (t/ha).

The same calculation runs for 1970–2000 and the four future periods of the chosen scenario. This gives the five bars and the trend sentence, which compares the best index of 1970–2000 with that of 2081–2100 (a change under 5 % counts as “about the same”).

4.3 Reading the result

  • Verdict: Excellent at 0.70 or more, Good at 0.45 or more, Possible at 0.25 or more, otherwise Poor (“struggles here”, with the reason: too hot, too cold or too dry).
  • Sowing window: every month whose index is at least 92 % of the best month, shown as ranges such as Oct–Nov.
  • Suitability map value = 100 × the best sowing-month index in each grid cell (land only).
  • Water message: the crop needs about X mm and local rain is about Y mm, followed by “enough”, “a little extra watering helps” or “too dry without watering”.

4.4 Worked example (illustrative arithmetic, not an app output)

Wheat has an 8-month season, a 450 mm requirement and a 5 t/ha potential. Suppose the season’s average temperature factor is 0.90 and 380 mm of rain falls. Water factor = (380 ÷ 450)^0.7 ≈ 0.89. Yield index ≈ 0.90 × 0.89 ≈ 0.80, which is “Excellent”. Expected yield ≈ 0.80 × 5 ≈ 4.0 t/ha, or 80 % of the crop’s potential.

In this model, cool-season crops such as garlic, strawberry and potato hold steady or improve, while warm-season, water-hungry crops such as maize, tomato and sugar beet lose potential, and sugarcane stays unsuitable. This is the kind of winners-and-losers picture the tool is built to surface. The absolute numbers are model estimates.

For the same point, the model gives 15.9 °C and 627 mm per year for 1970–2000. Under SSP2-4.5 it gives 18.3 °C and 600 mm for 2041–2060 and 19.2 °C and 590 mm for 2081–2100. Under SSP5-8.5 the 2081–2100 values are 21.4 °C and 565 mm, and under SSP1-2.6 they are 18.0 °C and 604 mm.

5. How the climate model works

Earth.exe computes climate at run time from a compact set of equations that imitate real patterns. Temperature and rainfall are generated for every grid cell, month, scenario and period, and every other layer is derived from those two.

5.1 Scenarios and timeline

The model keeps the end-of-century warming of four IPCC SSP scenarios (1.8, 2.7, 3.6 and 4.4 °C, which match the IPCC AR6 best estimates for 2081–2100 relative to 1850–1900). It ramps from about 1.5 °C in 2024 along a smooth curve, and then subtracts 0.35 °C to express change against the 1970–2000 baseline. The resulting base warming signal, before regional scaling, is:

5.2 Temperature

  1. Baseline. Warm at the equator, cooling poleward along a parabola in latitude (slightly steeper in the Southern Hemisphere).
  2. Seasonal cycle. The amplitude grows with latitude (0.25 °C per degree, so about 10 °C at 40°), is damped over oceans (×0.4), and follows the sun, reversed in the south.
  3. Climate-change signal. The base warming is multiplied by a regional factor, 0.85 + 1.7 × (|latitude| ÷ 90)^2.2, which makes polar amplification about three times stronger at the poles than at the equator. A land–ocean factor adds 1.25× over land and 0.8× over ocean, and a small seasonal term makes high-latitude winters warm more than summers.
  4. Regional texture. A gentle sinusoidal variation in longitude and latitude (about ±1.5 °C over land, ±0.45 °C over ocean) avoids perfectly banded maps.

5.3 Precipitation

  • Baseline of 15 mm per month, plus a tropical rain belt (peak 230 mm, about 11° wide) centered on a latitude that migrates ±8° with the seasons (the ITCZ), plus a mid-latitude storm-track band (peak 75 mm) near 50° in each hemisphere.
  • Land receives 85 % of the ocean rainfall.
  • Asian monsoon: an extra 230 mm peaking from June to September over 70–125° E and 8–32° N.
  • Subtropical deserts: rain cut to 12 % between 20° and 35° latitude (either hemisphere) from 20° W to 60° E, and to 40 % across the south-western North American desert longitudes (120–105° W).
  • Warming response: precipitation changes by 3.5 % × base warming × cos(5.5 × latitude), so the deep tropics and high latitudes get wetter while the subtropics and mid-latitudes (roughly 16–49°) get drier. The effect is slightly stronger over land (×1.1) than ocean (×0.8).

5.4 Derived layers

  • Sun power: extraterrestrial radiation from the standard FAO-56 equations (solar declination, Earth–Sun distance, sunset hour angle) for the middle day of each month, reduced by cloudiness, where cloudiness = min(0.95, 0.2 + 0.55 × P ÷ (P + 90)) and P is monthly rain. Radiation at the ground = extraterrestrial × (0.78 − 0.5 × cloudiness).
  • Soil wetness: rain over the last three months compared with a Hargreaves-type evaporative demand, mapped to 3–45 % by volume with 3 + 42 × (P ÷ (P + E + 1))^0.9 (land only).
  • Air humidity: 38 + 48 × P ÷ (P + 80), minus a heat term above 20 °C, plus a cold term below 5 °C, plus 12 over oceans, limited to 15–97 %.
  • Wind: a trade-wind band near 12° and a storm-track band near 50° latitude, scaled ×0.75 over land and ×1.35 over oceans. Under warming the storm track shifts poleward by 0.6° per °C of base warming.
  • Counting layers (frost, growing, pleasant, dry, hottest, coldest) are simple counts or extremes of the 12 monthly values.

5.5 Grid, interpolation and drawing

  • Fields are computed on a 1.5° grid (241 × 121 nodes, about 29,000 cells, roughly 165 km at the equator), with separate land and ocean values per cell.
  • For every screen pixel the app inverts the map projection, samples the field with bilinear interpolation and colors it through a 256-step lookup table.
  • The color overlay is drawn at reduced resolution (every 3rd pixel at rest, every 8th while dragging), then clipped to the land and ocean polygons. A 720 × 360 land-mask raster speeds up statistics, and d3.geoContains tells whether a clicked point is land.

6. How we built it

  • One self-contained file. About 0.7 MB, vanilla JavaScript, no framework, no build step, no backend, no API keys. The code makes no data requests and uses no cookies or browser storage.
  • Rendering. HTML5 Canvas 2D with D3’s orthographic projection for the globe and Mercator for the flat map, Path2D shapes, ImageData overlays and typed arrays (Float32Array) for the fields.
  • Performance. Computed fields are cached by (layer, month, scenario, period, difference mode, crop, watering); solar geometry is cached per latitude and month; the overlay drops to low resolution while the user interacts and returns to full resolution after 160 ms; hover and redraw work is throttled with requestAnimationFrame; canvases respect devicePixelRatio.
  • Interaction. Pointer Events handle mouse, touch and pen with two-finger pinch zoom; wheel zoom is anchored at the cursor on the flat map; the fly-to animation lasts one second with easing and handles longitude wrap-around; latitude is clamped near the poles; the URL hash (#climate, #crops) keeps pages linkable.
  • Robustness. Ocean points are handled explicitly (soil and crop layers are land-only), initial render and clipboard calls are guarded with try/catch, and difference maps use diverging color scales with their own legends.

7. Tools, languages, software and hardware

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript.
  • Libraries: D3.js 7.9.0 (orthographic and Mercator projections, geoPath, geoContains, graticule, geoDistance) and topojson-client 3.1.0, both loaded from jsDelivr.
  • Graphics: Canvas 2D for the maps and charts, inline SVG for the pixel sprites.
  • Fonts: Inter, DM Serif Display, Press Start 2P and VT323 from Google Fonts.
  • Hardware: none beyond a device with a modern browser; no GPU or special sensor is required.
  • Development environment and hosting: [add your editor, version control and the URL where the app is hosted].

8. Data, NASA and what is real

8.1 What the prototype contains

Two geographic datasets are embedded as TopoJSON: land polygons (L50) and country borders (C110) [confirm the original source and its license]. All climate values are generated at run time by the model in section 5. No climate dataset is stored or downloaded.

8.2 How NASA and IPCC science enters

  • The scenario framework (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5 from CMIP6) and its end-of-century warming levels from IPCC AR6.
  • Well-documented physical patterns of the climate system: polar amplification, faster warming over land than ocean, the seasonal migration of the tropical rain belt, monsoons, subtropical drying and poleward-shifting storm tracks.
  • Standard agro-climate formulas: FAO-56 solar geometry and a Hargreaves-type evaporative demand.

We did not ingest NASA datasets in this prototype. [If you used any NASA resource to study, tune or check the model, name it here.]

9. Limitations and validation

We state these openly because trust matters when people plan a harvest.

  • Educational prototype, not a forecast. The numbers are relative guidance. The app says so on the landing page, in the footer note and on every crop result.
  • Not yet validated against observations. The model has not been compared systematically with station or satellite data.
  • Local accuracy is limited. The grid is 1.5° (about 165 km) and the climate is generated from latitude-based patterns. For Zonguldak the model gives 15.9 °C and 627 mm per year for 1970–2000, with the same 52 mm of rain in every month. Observed station normals, for example from the Turkish State Meteorological Service (MGM), should be compared before using any number for a local decision.
  • No rainfall seasonality outside the tropics and monsoon belt. Mediterranean dry summers and autumn rainfall peaks are not represented yet.
  • Simplified crop model. Only monthly mean temperature and season rainfall are used. There is no soil type, pests, varieties, nutrients, CO₂ fertilization, heat waves, night frost or farmer adaptation, and each crop uses one global parameter set.
  • Watering is a fixed factor of 0.97. It assumes water is available, and in wet climates rain-only can score slightly higher than watering because rain-only is capped at 1.0. We plan to fix this artifact.
  • One model line per scenario. There are no ensemble uncertainty bands yet, and nothing beyond 2100.

10. Benefits and intended users

  • Farmers and cooperatives: see which crops hold up, which decline and which become possible; choose sowing months; judge whether watering is needed.
  • Agricultural extension officers and local planners: explain climate scenarios visually in a meeting or a field day.
  • Teachers and students: explore climate concepts interactively and export a CSV for lessons.
  • Developers and researchers: reuse the front end, since swapping the model for real data changes only the data source, not the interface.

11. Roadmap

  1. Replace the parametric core with real data (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, station-corrected baselines) and add multi-model uncertainty bands.
  2. Calibrate crop parameters by region with FAO crop calendars and yield statistics, and add early and late variety groups.
  3. Add soil and water realism: SoilGrids, SMAP-based soil moisture and irrigation limits.
  4. Add extremes from daily data: heat-wave days, late-frost risk and drought spells.
  5. Compare with recent seasons using MODIS and VIIRS vegetation indices.
  6. Improve access: Turkish and other languages, an offline-first web app, read-aloud and low-bandwidth summaries.
  7. Add saving and sharing: bookmarkable state and a printable planting plan.
  8. Run a validation study with local farmers and extension offices.

13. Quick start

  1. Open the app, press PRESS START, and choose Climate Map or Crop Finder.
  2. Climate: open ☰ Menu, pick a layer, a scenario, years and a month, click the globe, and read the Selected place panel.
  3. Crops: search a crop, tap its tile, tap a place on the map, and switch between Rain only and With watering. Use the menu to change scenario and years.
  4. Tips: try Play the year, Show change vs. the past, Land only, the 3D/flat toggle and the CSV button.
  5. Shortcuts: Enter on the landing page, Esc to close the menu, double-click to zoom, and the links ending in #climate or #crops.
